name: Dubai
tagline: Desert spectacle and skyline glamour at full throttle.
bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: Come November to March for temperate days, the racing season and Art Dubai in spring; avoid June to September, when the heat turns severe.

ourTake.lede: Dubai rewards travellers who look past the record-breaking numbers and treat the desert and the older creek city as seriously as the towers. Do the marquee sights (Burj Khalifa, the fountains) early or late to dodge both the crowds and the heat, and spend real time in a private desert camp and the Al Fahidi lanes, which is where the place actually breathes. Come between November and March; the summer is genuinely punishing and most outdoor pleasures shut down.
ourTake.comeIf: You want polished five-star ease, tax-free shopping and a beach-and-brunch rhythm three hours from home.
ourTake.skipIf: You are drawn to old-world texture, deep history or quiet, unmanicured places.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Le Royal Méridien Beach Resort & Spa
items.description: An established beach resort with gardens that have had time to grow.

items.name: FIVE Palm Jumeirah

items.name: JW Marriott Marquis Hotel Dubai
items.description: Twin towers on the canal, big, capable, and easy on the wallet.

items.name: Shangri-La Dubai
items.description: A calm Asian-service tower on the main road, understated by Dubai standards.

items.name: Burj Khalifa, At the Top
credentials: Guinness World Record, tallest building in the world
items.description: The world's tallest building at 828m. Ride to the Level 124/125 deck, or book the quieter, pricier At the Top SKY (148) or a private table at The Lounge on 152-154 for canapés and champagne well above the crowds. Time it for late afternoon so you catch the city in daylight and then lit up at dusk.

items.name: The Dubai Fountain
items.description: The choreographed fountain on Burj Lake shoots water up to 150m to Arabic and world music, on the half-hour every evening. Free to watch from the Waterfront promenade; for a calmer view, book a lakeside table at a Souk Al Bahar restaurant or a short abra ride across the lake.

items.name: The Dubai Mall
items.description: One of the world's largest and most-visited malls, and the anchor of Downtown. Beyond 1,200 stores it holds the aquarium, an Olympic-size ice rink, and the fashion-avenue luxury wing. A practical base for a multi-generation family: air-conditioned, endless dining including plentiful Indian and vegetarian options, and direct access to the Burj and fountain.

items.name: Museum of the Future
items.description: The torus-shaped building wrapped in Arabic calligraphy is a landmark in its own right, and inside it is Dubai's most imaginative attraction, immersive, theatrical exhibits on space, ecology and wellbeing. Book a timed slot well ahead; it sells out. Genuinely engaging for teenagers and curious adults.

items.name: Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque (day trip)
credentials: Guinness World Record, largest hand-knotted carpet
items.description: About 90 minutes from Dubai, and the single most beautiful building in the UAE, 82 white-marble domes, the world's largest hand-knotted carpet, and reflecting pools that mirror the whole structure at dusk. Free to enter; modest dress required and abayas are lent to women at the gate. Go late afternoon for the light.

items.name: Old Dubai by abra across the Creek
items.description: Cross Dubai Creek on a wooden abra for a single dirham, the oldest, most atmospheric way to move through the city. It links the Deira souks with Bur Dubai's heritage quarter, and shows you the trading port the whole city grew from. Do it early morning or golden hour.

items.name: Gold Souk
items.description: Hundreds of shops in covered lanes with windows stacked in gold, one of the largest gold markets in the world, and a rite of passage for Indian visitors who know their carat and their making-charges. Prices track the daily rate, so bargain hard on the workmanship. Best in the cooler evening.

items.name: Spice Souk
items.description: A short walk from the Gold Souk, narrow alleys heaped with saffron, dried limes, frankincense, cardamom and chillies. More about the smell and colour than serious shopping, though the saffron and oud are worth buying. Pairs naturally with the abra and the gold market for a half-day in old Deira.

items.name: Al Fahidi Historical Neighbourhood
items.description: Dubai's best-preserved old quarter, coral-and-gypsum houses, wind-tower coolers and quiet sikkas (lanes) from the late 1800s. Wander the galleries, the Coffee Museum, and courtyard cafés, then join the cultural centre's guided walk. A rare slow, shaded corner of the city.

items.name: Al Shindagha Museum
items.description: The UAE's largest heritage museum, a stretch of restored waterfront houses telling the story of the Creek, pearling, perfume and the ruling family, with modern interactive displays. More substantial and better curated than the old Dubai Museum, and an easy, cool, family-friendly cultural afternoon.

items.name: Atlantis Aquaventure & The Lost Chambers
items.description: One of the world's largest waterparks, with record-height slides, a shark-and-ray lagoon and a private beach, plus the adjoining Lost Chambers aquarium of 65,000 marine animals. The standout family day on the Palm; stay at Atlantis The Palm or Atlantis The Royal for direct access and skip-the-queue ease.

items.name: The View at The Palm
items.description: An observation deck 240m up in the Palm Tower, giving the one photo everyone wants, the whole palm-shaped island laid out below with the sea and skyline beyond. Quieter and cheaper than the Burj Khalifa deck, and the best place to actually grasp the scale of the Palm. Book a sunset slot.

items.name: Burj Al Arab afternoon tea or dinner
items.description: The sail-shaped hotel is off-limits unless you have a reservation, so book afternoon tea in the atrium's Sahn Eddar or a table at the Skyview Bar to actually get inside the icon. The gold-leaf interiors are deliberately over the top; go for the experience and the view, not restraint.

items.name: Platinum Heritage luxury desert safari
items.description: The discerning way to do the desert, vintage 1950s Land Rovers in a protected reserve, falconry, camel treks and a private Bedouin-camp dinner, run by one of the few licensed conservation operators. Choose a private vehicle to skip the dune-bashing party crowds; excellent for families and multi-gen groups.

items.name: Louvre Abu Dhabi (day trip)
items.description: Jean Nouvel's museum under a vast latticed dome that scatters a 'rain of light', a genuinely world-class collection spanning civilisations, from Da Vinci to regional antiquities. The building alone justifies the drive from Dubai. Pair with Qasr Al Watan or the Grand Mosque for a full Abu Dhabi day.

items.name: Qasr Al Watan (day trip)
items.description: The working presidential palace, opened to the public, a staggering display of domes, chandeliers and a mirrored Great Hall, plus a library and a genuinely good evening light-and-sound show on the façade. Dress smartly; it is a state building, not a theme park.

items.name: Jumeirah Mosque
items.description: One of the few Dubai mosques open to non-Muslims, via the Sheikh Mohammed Centre's 'Open Doors, Open Minds' guided tours where you can ask anything over Emirati coffee and dates. The most approachable window into local faith and custom, and beautifully lit at night from the outside.

items.name: Alserkal Avenue
items.description: A warehouse district turned contemporary-art hub, Dubai's serious galleries, artist studios, indie cinema, specialty coffee and concept stores, all in raw industrial units. Where the city's real creative scene lives, far from the malls. Check what's showing before you go; openings are the moment.

items.name: Jameel Arts Centre
items.description: A calm, well-funded contemporary-art museum on the Creek with rotating exhibitions, an art library, sculpture gardens and a rooftop. Free entry, rarely crowded, and a thoughtful counterpoint to Dubai's louder attractions. A good rainy-heat-of-day cultural stop.

items.name: Etihad Museum
items.description: Built on the spot where the UAE was founded in 1971, an elegant modern museum telling the story of unification through the original documents, films and the founding fathers. Compact, well-designed and the clearest explanation of how this country came to be.

items.name: Ras Al Khor Wildlife Sanctuary
items.description: A protected wetland minutes from Downtown where thousands of pink flamingos wade against a backdrop of skyscrapers. Free hides with binoculars look out over the lagoon; best in the cool winter months when migratory birds arrive. A surprising, peaceful hour for families and photographers.

items.name: Dubai Frame
items.description: A 150m golden picture-frame you ride to the top of, with a glass-floor skywalk and Old Dubai on one side, New Dubai on the other, the city's past-and-future divide made literal. Quick, cheap and photogenic; set inside Zabeel Park for a walk afterward.

items.name: Dubai Miracle Garden
credentials: Guinness World Record, largest vertical garden
items.description: The world's largest natural flower garden, over 150 million blooms shaped into arches, hearts and a flower-covered Emirates A380. Open only in the cool season (roughly November to May) and heaving with families; go on a weekday morning. Pure spectacle, and a hit with children.

items.name: Global Village
items.description: A seasonal cultural theme park where 90-plus countries set up pavilions of crafts, street food and shows, a lively bazaar-meets-carnival. Open winter only. Chaotic and fun for families and groups; a low-cost, high-energy evening with a strong South-Asian food presence.

items.name: Hatta (day trip)
items.description: A mountain enclave 90 minutes east, kayak the turquoise Hatta Dam, walk the 3,000-year-old Heritage Village, and drive the Hajar-mountain wadis. A complete change of scene from the city, cooler in the hills, and the closest real nature escape. Best October to April.

items.name: Ski Dubai
items.description: A full indoor snow resort inside a mall, real snow, ski and toboggan runs, and a colony of king and gentoo penguins you can meet. Absurd, and exactly why it delights children in the desert heat. Book the penguin encounter separately if that's the draw.

items.name: The Green Planet
items.description: An indoor tropical rainforest under a glass biodome, one of the region's largest indoor trees, sloths, snakes and free-flying birds across four humid levels. Compact, cool and hands-on; an easy 90 minutes that younger children love.

items.name: Ferrari World (day trip)
credentials: Guinness World Record, fastest rollercoaster (Formula Rossa)
items.description: The world's first Ferrari theme park, home to Formula Rossa, the fastest rollercoaster on the planet at 240 km/h. On Yas Island alongside Warner Bros. World and Yas Waterworld, so it anchors a full theme-park day for families with older kids and thrill-seekers.

items.name: Al Seef
items.description: A 1.8km stretch of Creek-front rebuilt in old-Dubai style, wind towers, sandstone lanes, floating market, cafés and abra stations, that flows straight into the historic quarter. A pleasant, walkable evening by the water with dhows drifting past. Family-friendly and easy.

items.name: Kite Beach
items.description: The best free public beach for activity, kitesurfing, paddleboarding, a running track and casual beach cafés, all with a clean sweep of Burj Al Arab views. More energetic and local than the resort strips; good for an active family morning before the heat.

items.name: J1 Beach
items.description: The Riviera-style beach-club strip that replaced La Mer, 13 upscale dining and beach-club concepts arriving from St-Tropez, Cannes and Tulum along a 500m shoreline. Book a daybed at one of the clubs for a polished, licensed beach day. The current centre of gravity for Dubai's beach scene.

items.name: Dubai Marina & JBR walk
items.description: Stroll the Marina promenade past superyachts and glass towers, then the buzzing beachfront of The Walk at JBR, full of cafés, street performers and people-watching. The most Miami-like part of the city; lovely in the evening. Add a short yacht or dhow cruise from the Marina to see it from the water.

items.name: Sunset yacht or dhow cruise from the Marina
items.description: Charter a private yacht (or join a smaller shared cruise) out past the Marina towers, Bluewaters, JBR and the Palm crescent as the skyline lights up. The private charter is the discreet, family-friendly choice, your own deck, catering and swim stop, away from the party boats.

items.name: Bluewaters Island & Ain Dubai
credentials: Guinness World Record, tallest observation wheel (Ain Dubai)
items.description: A polished dining-and-leisure island connected to JBR, dominated by Ain Dubai, the world's tallest observation wheel at 250m, a striking skyline landmark even when ride operations are paused, so check its status before counting on a spin. Come for the waterfront restaurants and the view of it either way.

items.name: Coffee Museum
items.description: A small, characterful museum in a heritage house tracing coffee across cultures, with antique roasters and a majlis serving traditional Emirati gahwa. A charming, quiet stop while wandering Al Fahidi, the kind of hidden gem that rewards the curious.

items.name: XVA Gallery
items.description: A leading contemporary gallery of Arab and Iranian art tucked into a courtyard heritage house, with a shaded vegetarian café and a tiny boutique hotel. An unhurried, cultured pause in the old town, art, mint lemonade and wind-tower shade.

items.name: Textile Souk
items.description: The covered fabric market on the Bur Dubai side of the Creek, bolts of silk, pashmina and embroidered cloth, and the landing point for the abra from Deira. Bring your bargaining; it's a lively, old-world stretch that pairs with Al Fahidi next door.

items.name: Al Qudra Lakes & Love Lake
items.description: Man-made desert lakes on the edge of the city, a cycling and picnic spot where you'll spot swans, oryx and migratory birds, plus the two intertwined heart-shaped Love Lakes. Cool, quiet and best at dawn or dusk; bring a car and your own supplies.

items.name: Deep Dive Dubai
credentials: Guinness World Record, deepest swimming pool for diving
items.description: The world's deepest swimming pool at 60m, built as a sunken city you dive or freedive through, with an underwater restaurant window. A genuinely unusual, bookable experience for divers and confident swimmers; sessions are limited, so reserve ahead.

items.name: Dubai Opera
items.description: A dhow-shaped venue at the foot of the Burj Khalifa staging opera, ballet, orchestras, musicals and big-name concerts. The most refined night out in the city, and a rare chance to dress up; check the season's programme and book a box for the fountain-side arrival.

items.name: La Perle by Dragone
items.description: Dubai's resident aqua-theatre spectacular, acrobatics, high dives and stunts in a purpose-built theatre with a stage that floods with water. Slick, wordless and family-friendly; the closest thing to a Cirque-style show in the city. Book weekend seats early.

items.name: City Walk & Coca-Cola Arena
items.description: A low-rise, European-style dining-and-shopping district that's pleasant to stroll on cooler evenings, anchored by the region's largest indoor arena for concerts and comedy. A relaxed alternative to the mega-malls, with wide pavements and good restaurants for families.

items.name: Sharjah Arts & Heritage Areas (day trip)
credentials: UNESCO, Sharjah named Cultural Capital of the Arab World (1998)
items.description: Twenty minutes north, the UAE's cultural capital, the Sharjah Art Foundation spaces, the excellent Museum of Islamic Civilization, and the restored Heart of Sharjah heritage quarter. A dry emirate and a serious, uncommercial contrast to Dubai's glitter. Half a day well spent for culture-minded travellers.

items.name: Dubai Aquarium & Underwater Zoo
items.description: One of the world's largest suspended aquarium tanks, viewable free from the mall or up close via the walk-through tunnel, glass-bottom boat and cage-snorkelling. An easy, reliable crowd-pleaser for children when you need an air-conditioned hour inside The Dubai Mall.

items.name: Skydive Dubai, Palm drop zone
items.description: A tandem jump over the Palm, freefalling with the whole island and coastline unfurling beneath you, arguably the most spectacular urban skydive on earth. No experience needed; book weeks ahead as slots go fast. The bucket-list thrill for adventurous visitors.

items.name: Mall of the Emirates & indoor entertainment
items.description: Beyond Ski Dubai, this is a genuinely upscale mall with a strong luxury wing, a cinema and VOX gold-class screens, and Magic Planet for kids. A cool-weather-independent day when the heat is punishing, with plentiful vegetarian and Indian dining nearby.

items.name: Palm Jumeirah Boardwalk & The Pointe
items.description: An 11km promenade along the Palm's crescent for a sea-air walk with Atlantis and the skyline in view, ending at waterfront dining. A calmer, free way to experience the Palm on foot, best at sunset when the light is soft and the heat lifts.

items.name: Emirates Palace & Presidential views (day trip)
items.description: The famously opulent palace-hotel where you can take the gold-flecked cappuccino and afternoon tea in the grand atrium, set in vast gardens on the corniche. A serene, monumental stop that rounds out an Abu Dhabi day alongside the Grand Mosque and Louvre.

items.name: FZN by Björn Frantzén
items.description: The Swedish master's Middle East debut, and one of only two three-stars in the city.

items.name: Trèsind Studio
items.description: The first Indian restaurant in the world to hold three Michelin stars, a matter of national pride.

items.name: Il Ristorante – Niko Romito
items.description: Romito's pared-back Italian ideal, on Bvlgari's island.

items.name: STAY by Yannick Alléno
items.description: Grand French dining, dessert library and all, in a garden setting.

items.name: Row on 45
items.description: A high, intimate counter where French technique meets Japanese omakase.

items.name: Ossiano
items.description: Dinner beside the aquarium wall, theatre that happens to be very good.

items.name: Moonrise
items.description: A rooftop counter for eight, the hardest, and warmest, seat in town.

items.name: Dinner by Heston Blumenthal
items.description: Heston's history-of-British-food, restaged with a Dubai view.

items.name: Al Muntaha
items.description: French cooking 200 metres up, inside the sail.

items.name: La Dame de Pic Dubai
items.description: Anne-Sophie Pic's delicate, aromatic French, translated to Dubai.

items.name: Smoked Room
items.description: Dani García's fire-and-smoke counter, Spanish, primal, precise.

items.name: Hoseki
items.description: A nine-seat omakase in a jewel-box room, the quietest luxury in town.

items.name: Jun's
items.description: Chef Kelvin Cheung's memory-cooking, Asian-American, personal, packed.

items.name: Orfali Bros Bistro
items.description: Three Syrian brothers and the most-talked-about kitchen in the Middle East.

items.name: Tasca by José Avillez
items.description: Portugal's finest, brought seaside, bright, generous, sunlit.

items.name: Hakkasan
items.description: The Cantonese standard-bearer, still holding its star after all these years.

items.name: Avatāra
items.description: A vegetarian Indian tasting menu that earned a star on its own terms.

items.name: Jamavar
items.description: The Leela's grand Indian house, newly starred in Dubai.

items.name: Manāo
items.description: A newly-starred Thai kitchen doing quiet, exacting regional cooking.

items.name: 11 Woodfire
items.description: Everything touched by fire, a chef's-counter ode to the flame.

items.name: Zuma
items.description: The izakaya that set the template for the whole city, still full every night.

items.name: LPM Restaurant & Bar
items.description: Riviera cooking and a room that has never gone out of fashion.

items.name: Gaia
items.description: Greek cooking with a designer's eye, as much scene as supper.

items.name: Boca
items.description: Sustainable Spanish cooking that quietly outclasses the district's louder rooms.

items.name: Mimi Kakushi
items.description: 1920s-Osaka glamour and Japanese cooking with real intent.

items.name: Bombay Brasserie
items.description: Grand Indian dining under the Taj's own roof, nostalgic and assured.

items.name: Bait Maryam
items.description: A Levantine home kitchen, run like family, because it is.

items.name: Lowe
items.description: Zero-waste, market-led cooking with a conscience and a sense of humour.

items.name: 3Fils
items.description: A tiny harbour-side counter that outranks half the city's grand rooms.

items.name: Kinoya
items.description: Soulful Japanese comfort food, ramen and izakaya done properly.

items.name: REIF Japanese Kushiyaki
items.description: Skewers over charcoal from a chef who made small food a big deal.

items.name: 21 Grams
items.description: Balkan home cooking with heart, the antidote to Dubai gloss.

items.name: Indya by Vineet
items.description: Vineet Bhatia's contemporary Indian, at a price that flatters the cooking.

items.name: Berenjak
items.description: Tehran's back-street kebab houses, recreated with real fire and flatbread.

items.name: Shabestan
items.description: Old-Dubai Persian dining on the creek, saffron and all.

items.name: Teible
items.description: Farm-to-table restraint in a design-museum setting.

items.name: Aamara
items.description: Indian cooking with a light, modern hand, Bib-listed and easy to love.

items.name: Revelry
items.description: A gastro-room that punches above its price, Bib-approved.

items.name: Hawkerboi
items.description: Southeast-Asian hawker flavours with real fire and swagger.

items.name: Sufret Maryam
items.description: Bait Maryam's sister, the same Levantine warmth, a lighter setting.

items.name: DUO Gastrobar
items.description: A neighbourhood gastrobar that keeps earning its Bib across outlets.

items.name: Bombay Bungalow
items.description: Beach-side Indian street food and curries, bright, fresh, unpretentious.

items.name: Konjiki Hototogisu
items.description: A Tokyo ramen name that earned its Bib on the bowl alone.

items.name: Hoe Lee Kow
items.description: Unfussy Asian comfort food with a devoted local following.

items.name: Al Khayma Heritage Restaurant
items.description: Emirati home cooking in a wind-tower courtyard house, the real old Dubai.

items.name: Goldfish
items.description: Sushi and seafood done cleanly and without fuss, a neighbourhood gem.

items.name: Khadak
items.description: Indian street-food energy, credentialed by the Michelin inspectors.

items.name: Harummanis
items.description: Malaysian home cooking, gently spiced, quietly excellent.

items.name: Skyview Bar, Burj Al Arab
credentials: Inside Burj Al Arab, global landmark venue
items.description: A drink 200 metres up inside the sail, the view most first visits are chasing.

items.name: Gold on 27, Burj Al Arab
credentials: Inside Burj Al Arab, signature high-concept cocktail bar
items.description: A gilded, theatrical cocktail room high in the sail, indulgence taken entirely seriously.

items.name: Mimi Kakushi
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars 2025 (No. 36), Best Bar in the Middle East
items.description: 1920s Osaka glamour and serious mixology, the most decorated bar in the region, and it shows.

items.name: Galaxy Bar
items.description: An intimate, constellation-lit room in the financial district, cocktails made with real intent.

items.name: La Petite Maison (LPM), bar
items.description: The Riviera room the city never tires of, a pre-dinner drink here is a Dubai ritual.

items.name: CÉ LA VI Dubai
credentials: Internationally recognised rooftop group, Address Sky View, 54th floor
items.description: The Burj Khalifa filling the glass, 54 floors up, the rooftop that best frames Downtown.

items.name: Above Eleven
credentials: World Luxury Restaurant Awards, recognised rooftop; established international name
items.description: A neon-lit rooftop with Peruvian-Japanese plates and skyline views, Bangkok's cult name, restaged.

items.name: Zuma bar
credentials: Zuma, MENA's 50 Best Restaurants; the district's benchmark bar-and-dining room
items.description: The bar that set the template for grown-up Dubai nights, still full, still faultless.

items.name: Gaia
credentials: MENA's 50 Best Restaurants (No. 35, 2024), DIFC's dressed-up late room
items.description: Greek glamour and a dressed-up crowd, as much a scene as a supper, well past midnight.

plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Cross Dubai Creek by abra to the Al Fahidi quarter, then coffee and cardamom at the Arabian Tea House.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Wander the gold and spice souks of Deira before the afternoon heat, then retreat to your suite at the Bulgari Resort on Jumeira Bay.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Ossiano beneath the aquarium at Atlantis, then a quiet nightcap on the terrace.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: An early, private ascent of the Burj Khalifa before the crowds, followed by the Dubai Fountain from the boardwalk.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Slow lunch and the collections at Jameel Arts Centre, then browsing the galleries of Alserkal Avenue.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Trèsind Studio, the city's three-Michelin tasting room, booked well ahead.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive into the Dubai Desert Conservation Reserve for a private falconry session at first light.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch and a long afternoon by the pool at Al Maha, a Luxury Collection Desert Resort.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A candlelit dinner in the dunes, then stargazing with an astronomer.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private yacht along the Palm and the Marina, swimming off the boat while the city is still cool.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at Nobu, then the Ottomans-to-orientalism rooms of the Etihad Museum.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at Row on 45, and drinks watching the skyline from Aura Skypool.

items.name: Downtown Dubai
items.description: For first-timers who want the Burj Khalifa, the fountains and the Dubai Mall on their doorstep; central but busy.

items.name: Palm Jumeirah
items.description: Beach-resort seclusion on the fronds, best for a slower, water-facing stay away from the city grind.

items.name: Al Fahidi and the Creek (Bur Dubai / Deira)
items.description: The old city of wind-towers, souks and abras, for travellers who want texture and history over gloss.

events.name: Dubai Shopping Festival
events.note: The city's biggest retail and entertainment season, with nightly fireworks, concerts and citywide sales.

events.name: Taste of Dubai
events.note: The city's flagship food festival, with restaurant showcases, chef demos and tastings across a weekend.

events.name: Dubai World Cup
events.note: The world's richest race day at Meydan on the last Saturday of March, a full dress-code social occasion.

events.name: Art Dubai
events.note: The region's leading contemporary and modern art fair at Madinat Jumeirah, anchor of Dubai's art season.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: For a first stay, Downtown or DIFC keeps you central; dress is relaxed but cover shoulders and knees in older districts and mosques. Alcohol is served freely in licensed hotels and restaurants, and Friday is the quiet day, with the working week running Monday to Friday.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Dubai International (DXB), most premium carriers use Terminal 1 or the Emirates hub at Terminal 3, where a Marhaba greeter can meet you airside and clear you through fast-track immigration before a chauffeured car handles the transfer.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Keep a private car and driver on call; the city is built around long air-conditioned drives, though Downtown, DIFC and the marina reward short walks after dark when the heat lifts.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Buy an eSIM (Etisalat/e& or du) before landing for instant 5G; hotel and mall wifi is fast and ubiquitous, and WhatsApp calling now works normally.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The dirham (AED) is pegged to the dollar; cards are taken everywhere, cash is rarely needed, and a 10 percent service charge is usual so tipping beyond a rounding-up gesture is optional.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: November to March is kind: warm days near 25-28C, cool evenings, low humidity. Avoid June-September, when heat tops 45C with punishing humidity that shuts down anything outdoors.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru, roughly 3.5 hours. Emirates flies it best in business and first, with complimentary chauffeur-drive at both ends; the A380 business bar is worth requesting on the wider-body rotations. Emirates First lounge at DXB is a destination in itself for onward connections.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required beyond routine; hepatitis A and typhoid sensible for any Gulf trip. Very safe, low street crime. Tap water is desalinated and safe, though bottled is the norm. Summer heat is the real hazard, not people.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Effortless for vegetarian and Jain travellers. Pure-veg and Jain menus are widely understood, and Indian food is everywhere. Rasoi by Vineet and the Jain-friendly kitchens across Bur Dubai are dependable; most fine-dining hotels will prepare Jain on notice.
